protocols.title: A patient is any human being who:
protocols.content:
Has a complaint suggestive of potential illness or injury that has resulted in a call for service
Requests an evaluation for a potential illness or injury
Has obvious evidence of illness, injury, cognitive impairment, or lack of decisional capacity
Has experienced an acute event or is in a circumstance or situation that could reasonably lead to illness or injury
Anyone who fits this definition must be properly evaluated, and appropriate treatment options must be taken, including obtaining an informed refusal that the competent patient does not wish to receive medical care, treatment, or transport.
For all patients who refuse emergency medical care/ transport:
In accordance with KBEMS, a patient has the right to refuse medical assessment, treatment, and transport even if their decision could be detrimental to their health. However, EMS personnel must ensure the patient has decisional capacity, understands the risks of refusing care or transport, and that the event is thoroughly documented.
Documentation Requirements
What is the medical complaint, injury, or call for service?
Does the patient or guardian have decisional capacity to refuse care?
Alert and oriented
Able to engage in conversation
Able to follow commands
Able to indicate an understanding of the situation
If allowed by the patient, a complete assessment and vitals, including a 12-lead EKG and blood glucose, if either is appropriate.
What are the potential risks and implications for not accepting medical care or transport by EMS? Also, what conditions and symptoms could be secondary to the incident that the patient should be aware of? Does the patient understand these risks?
What alternative options were given for treatment and transport?
Was there anyone on scene who was aware of the circumstances and could monitor, render aid, or transport if necessary?

protocols.title: The patient was advised to call 911 back if their decision to refuse care or transport changed or if EMS was needed for any reason.
protocols.content:
Procedure
Obtain all required information, including demographics, medical history, allergies, and prescription medications, as allowed by the patient.
Ensure that the documentation is completed with all requirements noted above addressed and any deficits thoroughly documented.
Refusal of care signature must be obtained, with a witness signature obtained if possible.
The following criteria must be present to withhold resuscitative efforts:
Unconscious / Unresponsive
No pupillary reflex
No carotid pulse
No respirations
Presence of asystole noted in 2 contiguous ECG leads.
Associated with:
Obvious mortal wounds (these include decapitation, incineration, hemicorporectomy, or injuries that are so extensive CPR cannot be effectively performed (e.g., severe crush injuries to the head, neck, or chest). Note that the presence of exposed brain matter alone is NOT an injury incompatible with life.
OR Rigor Mortis (this is stiffening of the body, usually occurring 4-10 hours after death. The exception is a patient exposed to cold temperatures.
OR Lividity/ Venous Pooling (a red/ purple skin discoloration that occurs when gravity causes the blood to sink to the lowest part of the body.  Lividity usually indicates that the patient has been dead for more than 15 minutes unless the patient has been exposed to cold temperatures.
OR the presence of a properly completed Kentucky EMS Do Not Resuscitate (DNR) form or Kentucky Medical Orders For Scope Of Treatment (MOST) form
If a person is dead at the scene, the responding unit shall convey this information to the communications center and request that law enforcement and the coroner’s office respond.  The area surrounding the corpse shall not be disturbed in any manner, unless it is necessary to do so to treat another sick or injured person.  When this is the case, any movement of the patient or items around the patient shall be documented thoroughly.
The body will not be searched for Identification. The EMS unit will remain on scene until contact is made with the coroner’s office representative (either in person or via telephone report) and the scene can be safely turned over to law enforcement officers.
The termination of resuscitative efforts is intended to be an event in which the EMS crew has undertaken resuscitative efforts and those efforts have been unsuccessful (except in cases where a person suffers from hypothermia, cold water drowning, lightning injury, or electrical injury). Termination of efforts is also appropriate when other conditions such as, but not limited to, the following exist.
Upon arrival to the scene, you find CPR is being performed on a patient who meets criteria for withholding resuscitative measures (Refer to page 9).
The patient is part of a mass casualty scene and has been triaged “Black”
The incident is unsafe, and the continuation of efforts will imperil responders’ safety
A condition exists that will impair your ability to transport the patient to a hospital in a safe and timely manner

protocols.title: You are presented with a standard form of identification of a patient’s desire not to be resuscitated in accordance with KRS 331.623 (DNR) or 201 KAR 9:470 (MOST)
protocols.content:
Paramedic:
If resuscitative measures have been initiated, the paramedic should consider termination of efforts prior to transport if the following are present:
Unknown or prolonged time of arrest to CPR initiation
Inadequate CPR prior to responders’ arrival
Arrest not witnessed by EMS
ACLS algorithm followed without clinical improvement >20 minutes
A minimum of 3 doses of epinephrine have been provided
Airway managed with advanced airway and ETCO2 monitoring
Reversible causes such as, but not limited to, hypoglycemia, overdose have been considered/ treated if applicable.
No ROSC has been achieved at any point during efforts.
The paramedic shall contact medical control for consultation via radio prior to the termination of resuscitative efforts.
The paramedic shall notify law enforcement, the coroner’s office, and follow procedure for scene preservation as outlined previously (Refer to page 9).
Major trauma patients may need to be transported to a designated trauma center in a timely manner.  It is in the best interest of the patient to be transported to a designated trauma center if the patient meets certain criteria.  In general, in the presence of significant trauma, consider the following:
Vital signs and consciousness
GCS < 6
SBP < 90mmHg (adult) < 70mmHg (< 9 years of age)
Respiratory rate <10 or > 29
Respiratory distress or need for respiratory support
Assessment of anatomy and extent of injuries
All gunshot wounds
All penetrating injuries to the head, neck, torso, and proximal ext.
Skull deformity or suspected skull fracture
Flail chest
Two or more proximal long bone fractures
Burns in conjunction with trauma
Any combination of 2nd and 3rd burns covering more than 10% BSA, burns to the face, or airway burns
Open fracture of a long bone
Crushed, mangled, degloved, or pulseless extremity
Amputation
Unstable pelvis
Active bleeding requiring tourniquet or wound packing
Mechanism of injury
Falls > 10 feet
Ejection from a vehicle
Death of an occupant in same vehicle
Prolonged extrication times with significant trauma
High speed auto crash indicators (Vehicle deformity or inturstion >12 inches)
Auto vs. pedestrian or bicycle with significant impact or victim has been thrown or run over
Pediatric Considerations
>13 years old with penetrating trauma or >15 years old blunt trauma
All other traumas, contact Children’s hospital downtown for guidance
If appropriate transport to level 1 trauma center and notify of impending arrival
Adult Medical

protocols.title: Guidelines
protocols.content:
Indications:
Non-traumatic abdominal pain including:
Appendicitis
Diverticulitis
Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm
Gallbladder Disease
Ectopic Pregnancy
Bowel Obstruction
Pancreatitis

protocols.title: Abdominal pain may be the first warning sign of catastrophic internal bleeding (ruptured aneurysm, liver, spleen, ectopic pregnancy, perforated abdominal viscus, etc.) Since the bleeding is not apparent, assume volume depletion and monitor the patient closely for signs of shock.
protocols.content:
Basic Care:
Administer oxygen if indicated – Titrate to >92% and work of breathing
Consider possible causes and follow other protocols as appropriate

protocols.title: Assess for hemodynamic instability, follow shock protocols if appropriate
protocols.content:
Advanced Care:
Establish IV/IO access with isotonic crystalloid solution to keep vein open
For mild to moderate nausea/ vomiting
Administer Ondansetron 4 mg IV

protocols.title: May repeat x 1 after 10 minutes
protocols.content:
Paramedic:
Moderate to severe acute pain >6 on pain scale
Consider pain management protocol
Administer Fentanyl 50 -100mcg IV/IO/IN
May repeat x 1 (Max dose 150mcg)
OR Ketamine 0.3 mg/kg IV/IO (May repeat x 1)
For severe nausea/vomiting that does not respond to Ondansetron:

protocols.title: Administer Droperidol 2.5 mg IV/IO (May repeat x 1)
protocols.content:
Indications:
Moderate aggression
Unable to comply with requests AND
Lacks decisional capacity AND
There is concern for dangerous medical conditions
Severe and dangerous aggression
Above are present AND
Poses imminent risk to self / others
Attempts at de-escalation have failed OR the patient is unable to comprehend verbal communication

protocols.title: High index of suspicion for a hypermetabolic state
protocols.content:
Basic Care:
Protect yourself and other crew members
Call for FD/PD assistance as indicated by the situation
Approach the patient in a calm/ cautious manner
Attempt verbal de-escalation first
Follow other protocols as appropriate for altered mental status and consideration of seizure, overdose, hypo/ hyperglycemias.
Administer oxygen if possible
Titrate oxygen to >92% and work of breathing
Initiate continuous EtCO2 monitoring if possible
Use physical restraint policy if necessary and as a last resort (Refer to page 111)
Physical restraint occurs in supine or lateral recumbent position only
Begin passive cooling if appropriate
Check blood glucose

protocols.title: Acquire 12-lead ECG if possible
protocols.content:
Paramedic:
Initiate cardiac monitoring if safe and appropriate.  All restrained patients must receive continuous monitoring of ECG, CMS, and EtCO2 for the entirety of the restraint period.
Moderate agitation/ aggression:
Administer Droperidol 5mg IM
If agitation/ aggression persists after 5 minutes
Administer Midazolam 5mg IM
Establish IV/ IO access with isotonic crystalloid solution to keep vein open (when it is safe and appropriate)
Consider fluid bolus of 500ml
Severe agitation / aggression:
Adminster Droperidol 5mg IM and Midazolam 5mg IM simultaneously
Closely monitor the patient’s airway and breathing utilizing EtCO2 following medication administration
Manage airway and ventilations as necessary
For sudden/ witnessed cardiac arrest consider
Early administration of Sodium Bicarbonate 100mEq IV/ IO

protocols.title: May repeat 50mEq every 10 minutes as needed.
protocols.content:
Indications:
Anaphylaxis is a life-threatening emergency that develops over minutes to several hours after allergen exposure and often involves:
Skin: hives, itching, flushing.
Airway / Respiratory: swollen lips/tongue/mucosal membranes, stridor, difficulty swallowing, SOA, wheezing.

protocols.title: Cardiovascular: hypotension with known allergen exposure.
protocols.content:
Basic Care:
Manage airway, breathing, and oxygenation as indicated.
Epinephrine is the most effective treatment for anaphylaxis. Aside from oxygen, epinephrine administration should not be delayed for delivery of other medications in this protocol.
Obtain complete set of vital signs, including SpO2.  Consider additional testing (e.g., 12-lead ECG) and monitoring (e.g., capnography) as indicated.
Remove inciting agent (e.g., bee stinger), if possible.
- Epinephrine:
Indicated for anaphylaxis with airway/respiratory involvement or hypotension with exposure to known allergen.
<30 kg: 0.15 mg of 1:1,000 concentration IM.  Repeat up to 2 times every 5-10 minutes, as needed.
≥30 kg: 0.30 mg of 1:1,000 concentration IM.  Repeat up to 2 times every 5-10 minutes, as needed.
Contact medical control for additional doses.
- Nebulized Albuterol:
Indicated for wheezing/bronchospasm.

protocols.title: 2.5 mg Albuterol (0.5% concentration) nebulized.  Repeat up to 3 times every 5-10 minutes, as needed.
protocols.content: Advanced Care:

protocols.title: Establish IV/IO access with isotonic crystalloid solution to keep vein open
protocols.content:
Paramedic:
Initiate advanced airway management as indicated and anticipate airway will be difficult to manage.
- Epinephrine:
Indicated for anaphylaxis with airway/respiratory involvement or hypotension with exposure to known allergen or recent (minutes) exposure to know allergen with high-risk features (e.g., history of near fatal or biphasic anaphylaxis, asthma/COPD, cardiovascular disease).
Patient weight <30 kg: 0.15 mg of 1:1,000 concentration IM.  Repeat up to 2 times every 5-10 minutes, as needed.
Patient weight ≥30 kg: 0.30 mg of 1:1,000 concentration IM.  Repeat up to 2 times every 5-10 minutes, as needed.
Contact medical control for additional doses.
- Epinephrine Infusion:
Anaphylaxis with impending airway/respiratory compromise or cardiovascular collapse or profound shock/hypotension that’s refractory to ≥2 IM epinephrine doses and fluid bolus.
Patient weight <30 kg: infuse at 0.1-1.0 mcg/min. (see Epinephrine Infusion protocol P. 133)
Patient weight ≥30 kg: infuse at 1.0-10.0 mcg/min (see Epinephrine Infusion protocol P. 133).
- Nebulized Albuterol / Ipratropium:
Indicated for wheezing /bronchospasm.
2.5 mg albuterol (0.5% concentration) and 0.5 mg ipratropium (0.02% concentration) nebulized.
Repeat albuterol treatments up to 3 times every 5-10 minutes, as needed.
- Fluid Resuscitation:
When indicated, administer 10-20 mL/kg isotonic crystalloid fluid bolus IV/IO (repeat x1 as needed).
Contact medical control for additional fluid bolus orders.
Frequently reassess and titrate to resolved hypotension and improved perfusion (e.g., more alert, decreased capillary refill).
Discontinue fluids if patient develops sign/symptoms of volume overload (e.g., new/worsening tachypnea, SOA, decreasing SpO2, new/worsening rales/crackles).
- Diphenhydramine:
Indicated for skin signs/symptoms.  Should never delay administration of epinephrine.
1 mg/kg IV/IO/IM.  Max dose 50 mg.
- Methylprednisolone:
Relatively slow-acting medication that can be considered for in addition to other therapies.  Should never delay administration of Epinephrine.
2 mg/kg IV/IO.
Patient weight <30 kg: max dose 60 mg.
Patient weight ≥30 kg: max dose 125 mg

protocols.title: -Note: Beta blockers and ace inhibitors may exacerbate anaphylaxis symptoms
protocols.content:
Indications:
Exposure to toxic substances from:
○ Ingestion
○ Inhalation
○ Injection
○ Skin absorption
○ Intentional/accidental exposure to pharmacological substances

protocols.title: Other medical conditions (see below) causing altered mental status
protocols.content:
Basic Care:
Remove patient from toxic environment as quickly as possible, remove clothing, and decontaminate if applicable
○ This should be performed by trained personnel with appropriate PPE
Administer oxygen
○ Titrate to ≥92% and work of breathing
○ Assist ventilations as appropriate
Initiate continuous EtCO2 monitoring
Follow other protocols as appropriate
○ Diabetic Emergencies
○ Hypothermia/Hyperthermia
○ Seizures/Status Epilepticus
○ Stroke/CVA/TIA
○ Trauma
○ Agitated/Aggressive Patient
Use patient and/or bystander statements and answers to determine if/what substances are involved
Determine blood glucose concentration and if <60mg/dL
○ Administer oral glucose 15g buccal, if conscious and able to tolerate
▪ If unable to tolerate oral glucose AND PATIENT HAS A PRESCRIPTION
▪ Administer Glucagon 1mg IM
Suspected opiate/opioid overdose
○ Administer Naloxone 2-4mg IN
May administer additional 2-4mg IN every 5 minutes to restore respiratory drive to max total 8mg

protocols.title:
Suspected carbon monoxide exposure
○ Monitor CO level if possible
○ Administer high-flow oxygen at 15LPM
protocols.content:
Advanced Care:
Establish IV/IO access with isotonic crystalloid solution to keep vein open
Blood glucose concentration is <60mg/dL
○ Administer Dextrose 50% or D-10, 25g IV/IO
May repeat x1 if no response
IV access cannot be obtained
○ Administer Glucagon 1mg IM

protocols.title:
Suspected opiate/opioid overdose
○ Administer Naloxone 2mg IV every 5 minutes to restore respiratory drive to max total 8mg
protocols.content:
Paramedic Care:
Begin advanced airway management as appropriate
Initiate cardiac monitoring
If signs of shock refer to shock protocols
Patient exhibits signs of organophosphate poisoning
○ Administer Atropine 2mg IV/IO
Repeat at 4mg every 3 minutes fully atropinized (secretions dried)
Suspected TCA overdose
○ Administer Sodium Bicarbonate 100mEq IV/IO
Suspected beta-blocker overdose
○ Administer Glucagon 3mg IV/IO
May repeat x1 at 2mg
Suspected calcium channel-blocker overdose
○ Administer Calcium Chloride 1g IV/IO every 5 minutes to max total 3g
Suspected dystonic reaction
○ Administer Diphenhydramine 50mg IV/IO/IM
Suspected adrenal crisis
AMS, hypoglycemia, hypotension, seizures, arrhythmias

protocols.title: Administer Solu-Medrol 125mg IV/IO/IM
protocols.content:
Indications:
Exacerbation of previously diagnosed asthma or COPD
Characterized by some combination of:
▪ Wheezing
▪ Tachypnea
▪ Accessory muscle use/retraction
▪ Inability to speak in full sentences

protocols.title: Wheezing due to suspected asthma or suspected COPD
protocols.content:
Basic Care:
Administer oxygen
○ Titrate to ≥ 92% and work of breathing unless COPD history
Oxygen administration in COPD patients:
○ Patient with history of COPD may have normal lower baseline oxygen saturation; do not automatically place on high-flow oxygen
○ Start 2-3LPM oxygen via nasal cannula
○ Titrate to patient’s baseline oxygen saturation or 88-92% and work of breathing
Initiate continuous EtCO2 monitoring
Acquire and transmit 12-lead EKG per 12-lead EKG procedure

protocols.title:
Wheezing /bronchospasm
○ Administer 0.5% Albuterol 2.5mg with 0.02% Ipratropium Bromide 0.5mg nebulized
▪ May repeat x1
protocols.content:
Advanced Care:
Establish IV/IO access with isotonic crystalloid solution to keep vein open
In addition to EMT DuoNeb, the AEMT may administer:
○ Additional DuoNeb treatments every 5 minutes as long as wheezing is present
Initiate cardiac monitoring
For moderate to severe respiratory distress
○ Initiate CPAP, per CPAP procedure

protocols.title: Discontinue CPAP if patient becomes hypotensive (SBP <100mmHg) Clinical picture worsens or initial presentation of impending respiratory failure
protocols.content:
Paramedic Care:
For severe respiratory distress that does not respond to previously indicated treatments.
Follow protocol for Respiratory Distress or Failure/Drug Assisted Intubation (See Page 39)
○ Initiate ventilations via BVM
For Subacute presentation
○ Administer Methylprednisolone 125mg IV/IO
○ Administer Magnesium Sulfate 2g IV slow push or for infusion (See Page 140)
Unable to cooperate or otherwise tolerate nebulizer therapy or impending respiratory failure
○ Administer Epinephrine (1:1,000) 0.3mg IM
May repeat after 5 minutes
Impending respiratory failure

protocols.title: Initiate advanced airway management per Respiratory Distress or Failure/Drug Assisted Intubation protocol (See Page 39)
protocols.content: Indications:

protocols.title: Heart rate less than 60 beats per minute with signs of hypoperfusion, including hypotension. Rates less than 50 beats per minute are more likely to be associated with hypoperfusion.
protocols.content:
Basic Care:
Place patient in supine or recovery position as indicated and tolerated by patient.
Obtain complete set of vital signs; including SpO2, blood glucose, and 12-lead ECG.
Titrate oxygen to a SpO2 of >94%; for COPD patients, consider titrating to SpO2 of 88-92%.

protocols.title: If signs of impending respiratory failure are present, initiate BVM assisted ventilation.
protocols.content:
Advanced Care:
Initiate 3-lead ECG monitoring and consider early application of defibrillator/pacing pads.

protocols.title: Establish IV/IO with isotonic crystalloid to keep vein open
protocols.content:
Paramedic:
Initiate advanced airway management as indicated and be prepared for post-intubation hypotension and/or worsening bradycardia.
Transcutaneous pacing:
Indicated for severe hypoperfusion +/- 2nd degree Mobitz II or 3rd degree heart block.  If present, don’t delay transcutaneous pacing (TCP) for IV placement or medication administration.
Consider sedation prior to TCP, if the patient isn’t at risk of impending cardiovascular collapse, or if purposeful movement affects ability to pace
Midazolam 2mg IV or 10mg IN  - May repeat x 1 in 10 minutes to maintain sedation
Initial settings:
Mode: sync/demand
Rate: 80 bpm
Current: start low and increase by 5-10 mA until mechanical capture is achieved (usually 40-80 mA).
Additional considerations:
Generally, the heart rate setting of 80 bpm is enough to produce adequate perfusion.
If capture is not achieved at current of 110 mA, consider repositioning pads and additional/alternative treatments.
- Atropine:
1 mg IV/IO.  Repeat x2 every 3-5 minutes, as needed.
Atropine is indicated for symptomatic bradycardia due to increased vagal tone +/- 1st degree heart block.
Ineffective for heart transplant patients, bradycardia due to hypoxia, 3rd degree heart block, and usually 2nd degree heart block.
- Fluid Resuscitation:
IV fluids can be used to treat hypotension (see Hypoperfusion Protocol Page 35), but should not delay or replace treatments that directly target suspected causes of bradycardia (e.g., atropine for increased vagal tone).
When indicated, administer 10-20 mL/kg isotonic crystalloid fluid bolus IV/IO (repeat x1 as needed).  Contact medical control for additional fluid bolus orders.
Consider Norepinephrine for persistent hypotension in the unstable patient (Reference protocol Page 148)
- Situations where additional/alternative treatments are often needed, include:
Beta blocker overdose:
Glucagon 2 mg IV/IO given over 1 minute.  Repeat dose x2 every 3-5 minutes, as needed.  Contact medical control for additional doses.
Calcium channel blocker overdose:
Calcium chloride 1 gm IV/IO slow IVP.
Hyperkalemia:
Calcium chloride 1 gm IV/IO slow IVP.
Sodium bicarbonate (8.4% solution) 1 mEq/kg IV/IO.  Repeat x1 in 5-10 minutes, as needed.
Severe / prolonged acidosis or sodium channel blocker overdose:
Sodium bicarbonate (8.4% solution) 1 mEq/kg IV/IO.  Repeat x1 in 5-10 minutes, as needed.
Symptomatic bradycardia refractory to TCP and/or other treatments:
Consider epinephrine infusion 2-10 mcg/min (see Epinephrine Infusion protocol page 133)
or

protocols.title: Consider push-dose Epinephrine 20 mcg slow IVP over 2 minutes.  Repeat every 3-5 minutes, as needed
protocols.content:
Indications:
- Respiratory distress in a patient with ≥1 of the following:
Clinical appearance of volume overload.
Suspected flash pulmonary edema / diffuse rales on exam.
History of congestive heart failure (CHF) with symptoms that feel similar.
History suggestive of volume overload (e.g., CHF patient that missed dialysis).

protocols.title: - The absence of peripheral edema does not rule out acute CHF exacerbation.
protocols.content:
Contraindications:
Systolic blood pressure (SBP) <100 mmHg (consider cardiogenic shock).
Clinical appearance suggesting asthma / COPD exacerbation.

protocols.title: Serious infection / sepsis
protocols.content:
Basic Care:
Titrate oxygen to a SpO2 of >94%; for COPD patients, consider titrating to SpO2 of 88-92%.
If signs of impending respiratory failure are present, initiate BVM assisted ventilation.
Obtain 12-lead ECG.
If chest pain or anginal-equivalent are present, follow Acute Coronary Syndrome protocol (See Page 29)
If appropriate, call for advanced life support, but do not delay transport.
If severe wheezing is present, consider nebulized albuterol 2.5 mg.

protocols.title: May repeat in 5-15 minutes as needed.
protocols.content:
Advanced Care:
Initiate EtCO2 monitoring.
Initiate cardiac monitoring.
If severe wheezing is present, consider nebulized albuterol 2.5 mg with ipratropium 0.5 mg.
May repeat albuterol every 5-15 minutes as needed, for a total of up to 3 additional doses.
If moderate to severe respiratory distress is present:
Initiate CPAP, as per CPAP procedure:
If signs of impending respiratory failure develop prior to or following initiation of CPAP, proceed to assist ventilations with BVM.
Discontinue CPAP if patient develops hypotension.

protocols.title: Establish IV access.
protocols.content:
Paramedic:
Treat dysrhythmia as appropriate.
Administer nitroglycerin (NTG) and titrate to SBP:
SBP >160 mmHg: 0.8 mg SL NTG every 5 minutes up to 3 total doses.
SBP 100-160 mmHg: 0.4 mg SL NTG every 5 minutes.
Assess blood pressure prior to repeat doses.
Do not administer NTG if patient has taken an erectile dysfunction medication (e.g., Sildenafil) within the last 48 hours.
Do not administer NTG if the patient is currently on an IV infusion for pulmonary hypertension.
If signs of impending respiratory failure are present, initiate BVM assisted ventilation and advanced airway management per Respiratory arrest/ failure/ DAI protocol. (Page 39)
*** Special Considerations ***
Assisting ventilations with BVM is indicated for patients with severe respiratory distress / severe hypoxia and not tolerating CPAP, peri-arrest state, or inadequate respiratory rate or tidal volume.
Multiple oxygen sources can be used to achieve desired SpO2 readings (CPAP + inline nebulizer or Non Rebreather Mask + NC).

protocols.title: Non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema (e.g., irritant exposure, post-opioid overdose) are not likely to benefit from nitroglycerin unless markedly hypertensive.
protocols.content: Indications:

protocols.title: Patient has a clinically significant glucose reading with an acute altered mental status.
protocols.content:
Basic Care:
Administer oxygen
Titrate to >92% and improved work of breathing
Initiate continuous ETCO2 monitoring
Determine blood glucose concentration
Relatively or clinically hypoglycemic, without concern of aspiration
Administer oral glucose 15g buccal until mental status improves

protocols.title: May repeat every 5 minutes as needed
protocols.content:
Advanced Care / Paramedic:
Patient is unable to tolerate oral glucose administration
Establish IV/ IO access with isotonic crystalloid solution to keep vein open
Initiate cardiac monitoring
For hypoglycemia
Administer Dextrose 50% (or Dextrose 10%) 25g IV/IO
If IV/IO access cannot be obtained
Administer Glucagon 1mg IM
For hyperglycemia

protocols.title: Consider 250-500 ML bolus of isotonic crystalloid for patient with severe hyperglycemia as appropriate to respiratory status (if no signs/ symptoms of pulmonary edema)
protocols.content:
Indications:
-Elevated body temperature related to heat exposure
-Altered mental status related to heat exposure
Mild Symptoms
Heat cramps, Heat exhaustion
No signs of altered mental status
Body temperature <104⁰F
Diaphoresis
Severe Symptoms
Altered mental status
Body temperature >104⁰F

protocols.title: Sweating may have stopped
protocols.content:
Basic Care:
Administer oxygen
Titrate to >92% and improved work of breathing
Initiate ETCO2 monitoring
Determine blood glucose concentration
Move patient to a cool place away from any external heat source if possible
Obtain patient temperature (Core temperature is preferred if obtainable)
Mild Symptoms:
Help facilitate passive cooling
Loosen clothing and remove excessive clothing
Administer PO fluids if available
Use caution if patient presents with nausea/ vomiting
Severe Symptoms:
Begin active cooling
On scene cold water immersion if possible
In transport continue cooling with directed air conditioning and cooled towels
Create mobile ice bath if possible (body bag filled with ice)
Place ice packs behind the neck, in arm-pits, and groin

protocols.title: If shivering starts, temperature drops below 102⁰ F, or AMS improves, stop active cooling
protocols.content:
Advanced Care/ Paramedic:
Establish IV/ IO access with isotonic crystalloid solution to keep vein open
Initiate IV/IO bolus of 500 ml for hypotension

protocols.title: May repeat up to max of 2L
protocols.content:
Indications:
Decreased body temperature related to cold exposure
Altered mental status related to cold exposure

protocols.title: Repeated ACLS medications and repeated defibrillations are ineffective below 86º F (core temperature)
protocols.content:
Basic Care:
Administer oxygen
Titrate to ≥92% and improved work of breathing
Initiate continuous EtCO2 monitoring
Acquire 12-lead EKG if indicated
Decrease ongoing heat loss as soon as possible
Move the patient to a warm area
Dry and insulate the patient
Handle the patient gently allowing the patient no exertion
Rough handling of a severely hypothermic patient may cause ventricular fibrillation
Remove all wet clothing (cut off to decrease patient movement)
Initiate passive external rewarming with blankets in a warm ambulance
Conscious patients should avoid heated oral fluids
Suspected severe hypothermia
Assess respirations and pulse carefully as both may be very slow but still adequate for the patient’s slow metabolism

protocols.title: Provide expeditious, non-emergency transport
protocols.content:
Advanced Care / Paramedic:
Severe hypothermia
Begin airway management as appropriate
Establish IV/IO access with isotonic crystalloid solution to keep vein open
Cardiac arrest
If a shockable rhythm is present, administer only one defibrillatory shock
Administer epinephrine (1:10,000) 1mg x1
Continue BLS CPR

protocols.title: If restored to a perfusing rhythm, follow the appropriate protocol
protocols.content:
Indications:
Non-traumatic chest pain suspicious for Acute Coronary Syndrome
Angina/myocardial infarction
Anginal equivalent symptoms (typically in the presence of risk factors for, or prior history of, Coronary Artery Disease)
Dyspnea (with or without exertion)
Light-headedness
Generalized weakness
Syncope or near syncope
Diaphoresis
Nausea and/or vomiting
Maintain a high index of suspicion for atypical presentations, e.g., diabetic patients or females

protocols.title: For any patient under 18 years of age, or for any patient being transported to a primary pediatric facility, MEDICAL CONTROL MUST BE CONTACTED PRIOR TO THE ADMINISTRATION OF ASPIRIN OR NITROGLYCERIN
protocols.content:
Basic Care:
Administer oxygen
Titrate to ≥92% and improved work of breathing
Initiate continuous EtCO2 monitoring
Acquire and transmit 12-lead EKG, per 12-lead EKG procedure
Administer aspirin 324mg PO (to be chewed)
Do not withhold unless known allergy or history of anaphylaxis
Administer nitroglycerin
If the patient has previously been prescribed, assist with administration 0.4mg SL every 5 minutes (Max 3 doses for BLS)
Titrate to SBP>100 and signs/symptoms (recheck BP before each dose)

protocols.title: Inadequate tissue perfusion manifesting as signs of hypoperfusion, including hypotension.
protocols.content:
Basic Care:
Manage airway, breathing, and oxygenation as indicated.
For suspected trauma, fully expose patient and control external bleeding.
Place patient in supine position or recovery position as indicated and tolerated by patient.
Titrate oxygen to a SpO2 of >94%; for COPD patients, consider titrating to SpO2 of 88-92%.
Obtain complete set of vital signs; including SpO2 and blood glucose.  Consider additional testing (e.g., 12-lead ECG) and monitoring (e.g., capnography) as indicated.
Consider causes of shock that have specific treatment protocols, including:
Poisoning/Overdose
Anaphylaxis
Symptomatic bradycardia
Adrenal crisis (acute adrenal insufficiency)

protocols.title: Tension pneumothorax
protocols.content:
Advanced Care:
- Initiate advanced airway management as indicated and be prepared for post-intubation hypotension.
- Fluid Resuscitation:
When indicated, administer 10-20 mL/kg of isotonic crystalloid solution IV/IO.  Repeat x1 as needed.  Contact medical control for additional fluid bolus orders.
Frequently reassess and titrate to resolved hypotension and improved perfusion (e.g., more alert, decreased capillary refill).

protocols.title: Discontinue fluids if patient develops sign/symptoms of volume overload (e.g., new/worsening tachypnea, SOA, decreasing SpO2, new/worsening rales/crackles).
protocols.content:
Paramedic:
- Norepinephrine Infusion:
Consider norepinephrine infusion, when distributive shock (e.g., sepsis) is suspected, other causes with specific treatment protocols have been considered/utilized, if there’s no improvement of hypotension/hypoperfusion with fluid resuscitation or the patient continues to deteriorate.
Frequently reassess and titrate to resolved hypotension.
See infusion protocol (See Page 148)
-TXA:
If catastrophic hemorrhage of medical origin is present, such as active GI or vaginal bleeding

protocols.title: Administer TXA 2g IV/IO slow push
protocols.content:
Special Considerations:
- Patients in 2nd/3rd trimester of pregnancy are at risk of developing supine hypotensive syndrome.  Consider placing in recovery position or manually displacing uterus to patient’s left.
- For shock resulting from trauma below the neck, especially penetrating trauma, consider titrating fluid resuscitation to the lower normal limit of the blood pressure range (e.g., 90 mmHg for 11-17 yo and adults).
- The elderly and patients taking cardiovascular medications (e.g., beta blockers, calcium channel blockers) have less compensatory tachycardia in response to shock and can deteriorate quickly.

protocols.title: - Adult patients with poorly controlled chronic HTN can have relative hypotension, which is a state of hypoperfusion at SBPs >90 mmHg.  Consider incrementally titrating to SBPs greater than 90 mmHg.
protocols.content:
Basic Care:
Administer high-flow oxygen if tolerated.
Initiate EtCO2 monitoring via nasal cannula
Check for vaginal presentation
If normal delivery appears imminent, follow childbirth procedure (Page 102)
Look for signs/ symptoms of obstetrical complications and treat as indicated
Conditions that prompt immediate transport despite the threat of delivery include:
Prolonged membrane rupture (>24 hours)
Breech presentation
Cord presentation
Extremity (Limb) presentation
Evidence of meconium staining
Nuchal cord
Breech presentation
If the infant’s head does not deliver immediately, place a gloved hand in the vagina with the palm towards the infant’s face
With the index and middle fingers, form a “V” n either side of the infant’s nose
Prolapsed umbilical cord
Insert two fingers of a gloved hand to raise the presenting part of the fetus off of the cord
Positioning the mother in knee-chest position may relieve pressure on the cord
Instruct the mother to “pant” with each contraction to prevent her from bearing down
Nuchal cord
Examine the infant’s neck for the presence of a looped (nuchal) umbilical cord during delivery
If cord is looped around the neck, gently slip the cord over the infant’s head
If unable to do so, clamp and cut the cord

Special Considerations:
Eclamptic seizures can occur up to 6 weeks postpartum but are most common 48 hours postpartum.
Most eclamptic seizures or signs of preeclampsia develop after 20 weeks gestation.
Signs of pre-eclampsia
Edema in the face, feet and/or hands.
Hypertension (systolic > 140 mmHg, diastolic >90 mmHg)
Headache
Blurred vision and or changes in vision
Eclampsia can occur without a previous diagnosis of pre-eclampsia.
Magnesium sulfate is the first line drug of choice when treating suspected eclamptic seizures
Pregnant patients or postpartum patients that are presenting with a blood pressure over 140 mmhg and/or diastolic over 90 mmhg or higher, coupled with other symptoms of preeclampsia should be treated with magnesium sulfate. These patients are at a high risk of progressing to eclampsia.

protocols.title: In the event of respiratory depression as a result of magnesium infusion the antidote is calcium chloride 1g IVP over 5 minutes.

protocols.title: Patient’s mental status may range from awake/alert to unresponsive

Provide ventilatory support as needed (Avoid hyperventilation)

protocols.title: See Page
protocols.content:
Basic Care:
Titrate oxygen to a SpO2 of >94%; for COPD patients, consider titrating to SpO2 of 88-92%.
If signs of impending respiratory failure are present, initiate BVM assisted ventilation.
Optimize patient positioning (ear-to-sternal notch and if no spinal precautions needed consider raising head of bed to ~45 degrees).
Use two-person BVM ventilation whenever feasible.
Have oral suction available, preferably large bore catheter (e.g., DuCanto Catheter).
Utilize airway adjuncts, especially for patients with facial hair, obesity, no teeth or protruding teeth.
Initiate EtCO2 monitoring and use to optimize BVM ventilation rate
Follow other protocols as appropriate, including:
Asthma/ COPD		CHF/ Pulmonary Edema		Shock/ Hypoperfusion

protocols.title: Allergic Reaction Poisoning/Overdose Hypoglycemia
protocols.content:
Advanced Care:
Initiate cardiac monitoring

protocols.title: Establish IV access
protocols.content:
Paramedic:
Consider reversible cause of patient presentation, including tension pneumothorax (see thoracostomy procedure page 109), opioid overdose, hypoglycemia.
For impending respiratory failure or anticipated loss of airway control (patient’s ability to protect airway), consider advanced airway management:
Nasotracheal intubation indications include:
Spontaneously breathing, unable to achieve sufficient facial / airway muscle relaxation, no sign traumatic facial instability.
Orotracheal intubation indications include:
Unconscious, no gag reflex, high risk for aspiration.
Time permitting, consider correcting hypotension (e.g., fluid bolus under pressure) prior to intubation.
Utilize airway management techniques (see Basic Treatment section) and consider oxygenating with two high flow sources (e.g., BVM and NC) to optimize SpO2 prior to and between intubation attempts.
Video laryngoscopy (VL) is to be used, unless equipment is damaged, not functioning correctly, or an appropriate size VL blade is not available.
The gum elastic bougie markedly improves oral intubation success rates and it’s routine use is strongly encouraged.
For placement of an endotracheal tube, an intubation attempt is defined as insertion of the laryngoscope blade into the mouth or endotracheal tube into the naris (opening of nose).
Intubation attempt durations should be no greater than 30 seconds and should be stopped sooner if marked SpO2 drop occurs during the intubation attempt.
Prior to further attempts, consider causes of failed attempt including:
Poor patient positioning
Need for different style of laryngoscope blade
Need for bougie
Facial / airway muscle tone too pronounced for oral intubation attempt in adult (need sedation)
If intubation unsuccessful after 3 attempts consider placing blind airway insertion device (BIAD), like the iGel.
Drug Assisted Intubation
RESTRICTED – GRADE 2 PARAMEDIC OR ABOVE ONLY
If unable to orally intubate adult patient due to facial/airway muscle tone and patient is at risk of aspiration or airway cannot be managed another way aside from intubation:
Consider drug assisted intubation (DAI) with Etomidate dose 0.3 mg/kg IV/IO (Max dose 20 mg) OR Ketamine 1.5mg/kg IV/IO
If insufficient relaxation, may repeat Etomidate at 0.1 mg/kg IV/IO. OR Ketamine at 1.5mg/kg IV/IO
If unable to intubate and unable to oxygenate / ventilate with BVM or BIAD, consider percutaneous cricothyrotomy
If sedation is required after successful intubation procedure and patient is     not hypotensive:
Consider Midazolam:
IV/IO:
Adult: 2-4 mg (Repeat in 10 minute intervals as needed)
Pediatric: 0.15 mg/kg (max single dose 4 mg)
IM/IN:
Adult: 10 mg
Pediatric: 0.15 mg/kg (max single dose 4 mg)
Repat IV/IO or IM/IN dose x1 in 5 minutes, as needed.
If Midazolam is not available, consider Lorazepam:
IV/IO:
Adult: 2 mg
Pediatric: 0.15 mg/kg (max single dose 2 mg)
After securing the advanced airway and verifying placement, attach device to ventilator utilizing Ventilator Protocol settings (Reference Page 102)
Rapid Sequence Intubation:
RESTRICTED – GRADE 3 PARAMEDIC ONLY
If all of the above procedures have failed to adequately manage and maintain the airway and it cannot be managed by other means, consider Rapid Sequence Intubation (RSI).
Cardiac monitoring, pulse oximetry, blood pressure, and continuous EtCO2 are required and must be documented.
All monitoring equipment should be placed prior to, during, and after any airway procedure
Pre-oxygenation
Position the patient supine in the sniffing position
Elevate the occiput so that the ears and sternal notch are parallel to the floor
Regardless of SpO2, place spontaneously breathing patients on a Non-Rebreather @ 15LPM
EtCO2 should be attached to the BVM circuit when in use
Preparation
Assemble all equipment (e.g. suction, BVM, CMAC, ET tube, bougie, stylet, SGA)
Establish and ensure patent IV/IO
Prepare Etomidate 0.3mg/kg
Prepare Midazolam 2mg
Prepare Succinylcholine 1.5 mg/kg
Assign team roles and perform verbal walkthrough of treatment plan
Apply nasal cannula 15lpm
Do not use a side-stream EtCO2 device
Induction
Administer Etomidate 0.3 mg/kg IV/IO AND Midazolam 2 mg IV/IO and flush with normal saline
Immediately administer Succinylcholine 1.5 mg/kg IV/IO and flush with normal saline
Continue to deliver pre-oxygenation during medication onset (45-90) seconds
Once the jaw is flaccid, perform laryngoscopy
If SpO2 drops below 93%, ventilate and oxygenate with SGA
Second attempt may be made once SpO2 is above 93%
If SGA unsuccessful, ventilate with two-handed BVM
If unable to oxygenate with the BVM, perform cricothyrotomy per protocol
Post-procedure
Confirm tube placement with EtCO2
If there is no waveform, the intubation is unsuccessful
Remove the tube and ventilate with SGA/ BVM
Assess for bilateral breath sounds
Secure tube with commercial device or twill tie
Document the depth of the tube at the teeth
If all other measures have failed to secure the airway and it cannot be maintained via other means for reasons such as:
Complete airway obstruction above the level of the cricothyroid membrane

protocols.title: Consider needle cricothyroidotomy (See page 104)
protocols.content:
Basic Care:

Initiate continuous EtCO2 monitoring
Position patient to avoid injury and / or aspiration
Consider placing patient in lateral recumbent position
Determine blood glucose concentration
Follow diabetic emergency protocol if indicated
Follow other protocols as appropriated for:
Trauma
Toxidrome/ Poisoning/ Substance Abuse/ Overdose
Obstetric Emergencies/ Eclampsia

protocols.title: Obtain 12 lead ECG if appropriate
protocols.content:
Advanced Care:
Monitor carefully for respiratory depression and need for assisted ventilation as appropriate
Consider airway adjuncts / ventilation

protocols.title: Establish IV/IO access with isotonic crystalloid solution to keep vein open
protocols.content:
Paramedic:
Initiate cardiac monitoring
If the patient is postictal or not actively seizing, pharmacologic therapy is NOT indicated.
Actively seizing or in status epilepticus:
Administer Midazolam 2mg IV/IO slow push
May repeat 2mg every 5 minutes as long as patient is actively seizing
May be given 10mg IN if unable to establish IV
For suspected pre-eclampsia / eclamptic seizure
Administer Magnesium Sulfate
4g IV/IO slow push over 3 minutes

protocols.title: Administer Midazolam 2mg IV or 10mg IN
protocols.content:
Indications:
Any positive finding on the modified Cincinnati Prehospital Stroke Scale
Facial droop
One side does not move or moves less than the other
Pronator drift
With eyes closed, patient is unable to hold both arms up equally for 10 seconds
Speech/ language deficit
Slurred speech, inappropriate words/ responses, or mute
Any score > 2 on the C-STAT stroke scale is positive for a possible large vessel occlusion stroke
Conjugate gaze deviation (2 points)
Eyes deviated in one direction or cannot cross midline
Level of consciousness (1 point)
Knows own age and month
Inability to close eyes and close/ open their hands
Arm weakness (1 point)

protocols.title: Unable to hold arms up for 10 seconds
protocols.content:
Basic Care:
Administer oxygen
Titrate to >92% and improved work of breathing
Initiate continuous EtCO2 monitoring
Determine blood glucose concentration and follow diabetic emergencies protocol as appropriate
When possible, transport a witness of the onset of symptoms in the ambulance to assist the receiving facility in determining care plan OR
Obtain a phone number from reliable witness for hospital contact
Initiate airway management measures with adjunct and BVM as appropriate
Contact receiving facility and provide notification of stroke alert

protocols.title: Initiate rapid, immediate transport

protocols.title: Establish IV/ IO access with isotonic crystalloid solution to keep vein open.  Do not delay transport for IV access.

Paramedic:
Initiate advanced airway management as appropriate

protocols.title: Initiate cardiac monitoring and acquire a 12-lead ECG
protocols.content:
Indications:
Signs/ symptoms directly attributable to tachydysrhythmias typically do  not appear until the heart rate is > 150bpm.

Chest pain
Diaphoresis
Hypotension
Altered level of consciousness
ACS/ Acute MI

protocols.content:

Assess for hemodynamic instability

protocols.title: May repeat fluid bolus if no signs of fluid overload are present
protocols.content:
Paramedic:
Initiate cardiac monitoring.  Evaluate rhythm for width, regularity, and rate
Do not delay cardioversion in the presence of hemodynamic instability
Apply defibrillation pads
Consider sedation prior to cardioversion if time and patient’s condition permits
Administer Midazolam 2mg IV/IO OR 10mg IN
OR Consider Ketamine 0.3mg/kg IV/IO
Unstable
Narrow complex (QRS <0.12 seconds)
Regular (SVT, PAT, or atrial flutter)
Synchronized cardioversion: 100J then (if no response) 200J, 300J, 360J
When preparing for cardioversion, administer Adenosine 12mg IV/IO rapid push with saline flush.
May repeat Adenosine 12mg once after 2 minutes if needed
Irregular (atrial fibrillation)
Synchronized cardioversion: 100J, then (if no response) 200J, 300J, 360J
Wide complex (QRS >0.12 seconds)
Regular (VT or possible SVT with aberrancy or underlying BBB/IVCD)
Synchronized cardioversion: 100J, then (if no response) 200J, 300J, 360J
Irregular (atrial fibrillation with aberrancy or BBB, IVCD)
Synchronized cardioversion: 100J, then (if no response) 200J, 300J, 360J
Stable
Narrow complex (QRS <0.12 seconds)
Regular (SVT/ presumed PAT)
Perform vagal maneuvers
If no response, administer Adenosine 12mg IV/IO rapid push with saline flush
Repeat same dose after 2 minutes if no response
Irregular (Atrial fibrillation)
Administer Diltiazem 0.25mg/kg (max 20mg) IV slow push over five minutes
If no response, administer Diltiazem 0.35mg/kg (max 35mg) IV slow push over 5 minutes
If rate control achieved, initiate Diltiazem infusion 5mg/hour IV (See Pharmacopeia Page 129)
Wide complex (QRS >0.12 seconds)
Regular (VT, possible SVT with aberrancy of underlying BBB/ IVCD) WITH A PULSE
Administer Amiodarone 150mg IV/IO over 10 minutes OR
Administer Lidocaine 100mg IV/IO
Presumed hyperkalemia
Administer Calcium Chloride 1g IV slow push every 5 minutes to max total of 3g
Administer 8.4% solution Sodium Bicarbonate 100mEq
Polymorphic VT (Torsades de Pointes)
Administer Magnesium Sulfate 2mg IV/IO slow push over 2 minutes
Irregular
Monitor and transport.  Be vigilant for deterioration to VF/ VT
Adult Trauma

Control bleeding with direct pressure and elevation if possible
Cover the stump with moist, sterile gauze then wrap with dry dressing

Do not place directly in ice or submerge/ soak in water

Administer oxygen

Initiate continuous EtCO2 monitoring
Begin airway management as appropriate
Obtain 12-lead ECG, especially when injury involves electrical burns
Monitor CO level if possible
Stop the burning process
Remove dry chemicals and flush affected area with copious amounts of water
Remove contaminated clothing

protocols.content:
Paramedic:
Patients receiving the medications listed below should be closely observed with monitoring of BP, Heart rate, EtCO2, airway patency, breathing status, and circulation.
Severe pain:
Fentanyl
IV/IO: 1 mcg/kg slow push
Adult max single dose 100 mcg.

Coadministration (never in same syringe) of Ketamine and Fentanyl may enhance the beneficial effects of these medications but may also enhance adverse effects like respiratory depression.
