protocols.title: For respiratory depression associated with fentanyl treatment, manage the airway / breathing and administer naloxone 0.4-2 mg IV/IO/IM/IN titrated to respiratory status.
protocols.content:
Basic Care:
Ensure the airway is patent while protecting the cervical spine
Evaluate for and treat exsanguinating hemorrhage
Initiate oxygen therapy with continuous EtCO2 monitoring
Begin airway management as appropriate
Treat injuries and control bleeding as needed including wound packing, and / or tourniquet application
Determine the need for C-Spine immobilization per selective spinal immobilization procedure (See Page 113)
C-Spine immobilization is not indicated for penetrating trauma unless a neurological deficit is noted on assessment
Assess for hemodynamic instability and follow shock protocol if indicated
Head and neck injuries:
Determine the need for C-Spine immobilization
Chest injuries:
Control bleeding
Stabilize impaled objects without removing them
Cover open chest wounds with occlusive dressing
Evaluate the back for wounds (potential for entrance/exit of GSW)
Abdominal injuries:
Control bleeding
Stabilize impaled objects
Cover eviscerations with moist, sterile gauze
Extremity injuries:
Splint according to injury type and location
Apply sterile dressings to open fractures.  Do not replace exposed bone.
Control bleeding with direct pressure and/ or tourniquet
Do not attempt to reduce dislocations in the field
Pregnant patients:
If major trauma to the abdomen, suspect life-threatening injuries
In general, the fluid filled uterus protects the fetus from blunt trauma, but these patients should be transported for evaluation.
Direct trauma may result in premature separation of the placenta from the uterine wall, premature labor, uterine rupture, abortion, or fetal death.
Place patient in left lateral recumbent position

protocols.title: When determining receiving facility, trauma takes precedent over the patient’s OB hospital of choice.
protocols.content:
Advanced Care:
Establish IV/IO access with isotonic crystalloid solution to keep vein open

protocols.title: Consider a 2nd IV site for fluid resuscitation if signs of decompensation or hypotension
protocols.content:
Paramedic:
Begin advanced airway management if indicated (Page 39)
Initiate continuous cardiac monitoring
Consider pain management protocol as appropriate with Fentanyl or Ketamine (Page 51)
Consider needle thoracostomy for suspected pneumothorax (Page 109)
Significant bleeding:
Administer TXA 2g IV/IO slow push
Significant crush injury, suspected rhabdomyolysis
Administer Sodium Bicarbonate 1mEq/Kg (Max 50 mEq) slow IV push
Monitor ECG before and after freeing patient from crushing injury
If hyperkalemia develops

protocols.title: Administer Calcium Chloride 1Gm IV/IO slow IV push
protocols.content: Indications:

protocols.title: Inadequate tissue perfusion manifesting as signs of hypoperfusion, including hypotension.
protocols.content:
Basic Care:
- Manage airway, breathing, and oxygenation as indicated.
- For suspected trauma, fully expose patient and control external bleeding.
- Place patient in supine position or recovery position as indicated and tolerated by patient.
- Titrate oxygen to a SpO2 of >94%; for COPD patients, consider titrating to SpO2 of 88-92%.
- Obtain complete set of vital signs; including SpO2 and blood glucose.  Consider additional testing (e.g., 12-lead ECG) and monitoring (e.g., capnography) as indicated.
- Consider causes of shock that have specific treatment protocols, including:
Poisoning/Overdose
Anaphylaxis
Symptomatic bradycardia
Adrenal crisis (acute adrenal insufficiency)

protocols.title: Tension pneumothorax
protocols.content:
Advanced Care:
- Initiate advanced airway management as indicated and be prepared for post-intubation hypotension.
- Fluid Resuscitation:
When indicated, administer 10-20 mL/kg isotonic crystalloid solution IV/IO.  Repeat x1 as needed.  Contact medical control for additional fluid bolus orders.
Frequently reassess and titrate to resolved hypotension and improved perfusion (e.g., more alert, decreased capillary refill).

protocols.title: Discontinue fluids if patient develops sign/symptoms of volume overload (e.g., new/worsening tachypnea, SOA, decreasing SpO2, new/worsening rales/crackles).
protocols.content:
Paramedic:
- Norepinephrine Infusion:
Consider norepinephrine infusion, when distributive shock (e.g., sepsis) is suspected, other causes with specific treatment protocols have been considered/utilized, if there’s no improvement of hypotension/hypoperfusion with fluid resuscitation or the patient continues to deteriorate.
Frequently reassess and titrate to resolved hypotension.
See infusion chart Page 148
-TXA:
If catastrophic hemorrhage of medical origin is present, such as active GI or vaginal bleeding

protocols.title: Administer TXA 2g IV/IO slow push
protocols.content:
Special Considerations:
- Patients in 2nd/3rd trimester of pregnancy are at risk of developing supine hypotensive syndrome.  Consider placing in recovery position or manually displacing uterus to patient’s left.
- For shock resulting from trauma below the neck, especially penetrating trauma, consider titrating fluid resuscitation to the lower normal limit of the blood pressure range (e.g., 90 mmHg for 11-17 yo and adults).
- The elderly and patients taking cardiovascular medications (e.g., beta blockers, calcium channel blockers) have less compensatory tachycardia in response to shock and can deteriorate quickly.

protocols.title: - Adult patients with poorly controlled chronic HTN can have relative hypotension, which is a state of hypoperfusion at SBPs >90 mmHg.  Consider incrementally titrating to SBPs greater than 90 mmHg.
protocols.content: Indications:

protocols.title: Patient is in cardiac arrest that is believed to be traumatic in nature
protocols.content:
Basic Care:
If patient presentation meets requirements outlined in Withholding Resuscitative Measures protocol (Page 9), do NOT attempt resuscitation
Pregnant female at / more than 24 weeks estimated gestation or uterine fundus palpable above the umbilicus:
Initiate IMMEDIATE TRANSPORT to nearest hospital with OBGYN services (Preferably level 1 trauma center if other trauma is present)
Follow additional protocol for resuscitation en route to facility
In all other cases: Begin CPR immediately
Apply AED and perform a rhythm analysis as soon as possible while limiting interruptions in CPR for analysis / shock period only
Insert blind supraglottic airway device (I-gel) and provide ventilations with continuous EtCO2 monitoring
Control external hemorrhage
Use tourniquets if needed
Apply pelvic binder for blunt trauma, if indicated

protocols.title: Apply Lucas device after 2nd rhythm analysis/ shock period and set to deliver continuous compressions
protocols.content:
Advanced Care:
Place patient on 3-lead ECG for continuous monitoring
Analyze patient at 2-minute intervals and follow AED prompts for defibrillation
Establish IV/IO access with isotonic crystalloid solution to keep vein open
Provide Epinephrine 1mg (1:10000) IV/ IO every 3-5 minutes for duration of arrest period
Initiate fluid bolus 500 mL

protocols.title: Consider non-traumatic causes / treatments as warranted
protocols.content:
Paramedic:
Treat severe hemorrhagic shock as indicated above
Severe bleeding:
Administer TXA 2g IV/IO slow push
Treat obstructive shock
Perform needle thoracostomy as indicated for tension pneumothorax
Perform rhythm analysis after every 2 minutes of continuous CPR
For ventricular fibrillation/ ventricular tachycardia
Defibrillate as soon as rhythm identified
Consider Amiodarone for recurrent v-tach, Calcium for Hyperkalemia, Lidocaine if V-tach persists after Amiodarone, or Magnesium for Torsades.  See Pharmacopeia for more.
Initiate transport to Level 1 trauma center
For Asystole or pulseless electrical activity with rate <40 BPM
Continue CPR without defibrillation
If no change / improvement following 20 minutes of continuous care:
Contact medical control per Termination of Efforts protocol (See page 10)
If ROSC achieved:
Follow ROSC protocol (See Page 38)
Initiate transport to Level 1 trauma center
Perform endotracheal intubation and utilize ventilator
Ensure hemorrhage control
Ensure bilateral chest rise and fall
Consider repeat chest decompression
Consider repeat fluid bolus
Pediatric Medical

protocols.title: Guidelines
protocols.content:
Indications:
Non-traumatic abdominal pain including:
Appendicitis
Severe constipation
Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm
Gastroenteritis
Bowel Obstruction
Pancreatitis

protocols.title: Abdominal pain may be the first warning sign of catastrophic internal bleeding (ruptured aneurysm, liver, spleen, ectopic pregnancy, perforated abdominal viscus, etc.) Since the bleeding is not apparent, you must think of volume depletion and monitor the patient closely to recognize shock.
protocols.content:
Basic Care:
Consult age based guide, such as Handtevy app, for appropriate medication doses/interventions/equipment sizes and reference to normal vital sign ranges for pediatric patients
Administer oxygen if indicated - Titrate to >95% and improved work of breathing
Consider possible causes and follow other protocols as appropriate

protocols.title: Assess for hemodynamic instability, follow shock protocols if appropriate
protocols.content:
Advanced Care:
Establish IV/IO access with isotonic crystalloid solution to keep vein open
For mild to moderate nausea/ vomiting:
Administer Ondanestron 0.1mg/kg OR 4mg SL (if >4 years of age)

protocols.title: May repeat x 1 after 10 minutes not to exceed 4mg total
protocols.content:
Paramedic:
Moderate to severe acute pain >6 on pain scale
Consider pain management protocol
Administer Fentanyl 1mcg/kg IV OR 1.5mcg/kg IN (max single dose 50mcg) (May repeat x 1 after 10 minutes)

protocols.title: OR Ketamine 0.3mg/kg IV/IO (May repeat x 1 after 10 minutes)
protocols.content:
Indications:
Anaphylaxis is a life-threatening emergency that develops over minutes to several hours after allergen exposure and often involves:
Skin: hives, itching, flushing.
Airway / Respiratory: swollen lips/tongue/mucosal membranes, stridor, difficulty swallowing, SOA, wheezing.

protocols.title: Cardiovascular: hypotension with known allergen exposure.
protocols.content:
Basic Care:
Consult age-based guide, such as Handtevy app, for appropriate medication doses/interventions/equipment sizes and reference to normal vital sign ranges for pediatric patients
Manage airway, breathing, and oxygenation as indicated.
Epinephrine is the most effective treatment for anaphylaxis. Aside from oxygen, epinephrine administration should not be delayed for delivery of other medications in this protocol.
Obtain complete set of vital signs, including SpO2.  Consider additional testing (e.g., 12-lead ECG) and monitoring (e.g., capnography) as indicated.
Remove inciting agent (e.g., bee stinger), if possible.
For anaphylaxis with airway/respiratory involvement or hypotension with exposure to known allergen:
Administer Epinephrine (1:1000)
<30 kg: 0.15 mg of 1:1000 concentration IM.  Repeat x2 every 5-10 minutes, as needed.
≥30 kg: 0.30 mg of 1:1000 concentration IM.  Repeat x2 every 5-10 minutes, as needed.
Contact medical control for additional doses.
For Wheezing/ Bronchospasm:

protocols.title: Administer 2.5 mg albuterol (0.5% concentration) nebulized.  Repeat x1 after 5 minutes, as needed.
protocols.content: Advanced Care:

protocols.title: Establish IV/IO access with isotonic crystalloid solution to keep vein open
protocols.content:
Paramedic:
Initiate advanced airway management as indicated and anticipate airway will be difficult to manage.
- Epinephrine:
Indicated for anaphylaxis with airway/respiratory involvement or hypotension with exposure to known allergen or recent (minutes) exposure to know allergen with high-risk features (e.g., history of near fatal or biphasic anaphylaxis, asthma/COPD, cardiovascular disease).
Patient weight <30 kg: 0.15 mg of 1:1,000 concentration IM.  Repeat x2 every 5-10 minutes, as needed.
Patient weight ≥30 kg: 0.30 mg of 1:1,000 concentration IM.  Repeat x2 every 5-10 minutes, as needed.
Contact medical control for additional doses.
- Epinephrine Infusion:
Anaphylaxis with impending airway/respiratory compromise or cardiovascular collapse or profound shock/hypotension that’s refractory to ≥2 IM epinephrine doses and fluid bolus.
Patient weight <30 kg: infuse at 0.1-1.0 mcg/min. (see Epinephrine Infusion protocol Page 133).
Patient weight ≥30 kg: infuse at 1.0-10.0 mcg/min (see Epinephrine Infusion protocol Page 133).
- Nebulized albuterol / ipratropium:
Indicated for wheezing /bronchospasm.
2.5 mg albuterol (0.5% concentration) and 0.5 mg ipratropium (0.02% concentration) nebulized.
Repeat albuterol treatments x3 every 5-10 minutes, as needed.
- Fluid Resuscitation:
When indicated, administer 10-20 mL/kg isotonic crystalloid solution IV/IO (repeat x1 as needed).
Contact medical control for additional fluid bolus orders.
Frequently reassess and titrate to resolved hypotension and improved perfusion (e.g., more alert, decreased capillary refill).
Discontinue fluids if patient develops sign/symptoms of volume overload (e.g., new/worsening tachypnea, SOA, decreasing SpO2, new/worsening rales/crackles).
- Diphenhydramine:
Indicated for skin signs/symptoms.  Should never delay administration of epinephrine.
1 mg/kg IV/IO/IM.  Max dose 50 mg.
- Methylprednisolone:
Relatively slow-acting medication that can be considered for in addition to other therapies.  Should never delay administration of epinephrine.
2 mg/kg IV/IO.
Patient weight <30 kg: max dose 60 mg.

protocols.title: Patient weight ≥30 kg: max dose 125 mg.
protocols.content:
Indications:
Exposure to toxic substances from:
○ Ingestion
○ Inhalation
○ Injection
○ Skin absorption
○ Intentional/accidental exposure to pharmacological substances

protocols.title: Other medical conditions (see below) causing altered mental status
protocols.content:
Basic Care:
Remove patient from toxic environment as quickly as possible, remove clothing, and decontaminate if applicable
○ This should be performed by trained personnel with appropriate PPE
Administer oxygen
○ Titrate to ≥95% and work of breathing
○ Assist ventilations as appropriate
Initiate continuous EtCO2 monitoring
Follow other protocols as appropriate
○ Diabetic Emergencies
○ Hypothermia/Hyperthermia
○ Seizures/Status Epilepticus
○ Stroke/CVA/TIA
○ Trauma
○ Agitated/Aggressive Patient
Use patient and/or bystander statements and answers to determine if/what substances are involved
Determine blood glucose concentration and if <60mg/dL
○ Administer oral glucose 15g buccal, if conscious and able to tolerate
If unable to tolerate oral glucose AND PATIENT HAS A PRESCRIPTION
▪ Administer Glucagon 0.1mg/kg IM (Max 1mg)
Suspected opiate/opioid overdose
○ Administer naloxone 0.1mg/kg IN
May administer additional Naloxone 0.1mg/kg IN every 5 minutes to restore respiratory drive to max total 2mg

protocols.title:
Suspected carbon monoxide exposure
○ Monitor CO level if possible
○ Administer high-flow oxygen at 15LPM
protocols.content:
Advanced Care:
Establish IV/IO access with isotonic crystalloid solution to keep vein open
Blood glucose concentration is <60mg/dL
○ Administer dextrose 10% 4ml/kg  IV/IO
May repeat x1 if no response
IV access cannot be obtained
○ Administer Glucagon 0.1mg/kg IM (Max 1mg)

protocols.title:
Suspected opiate/opioid overdose
○ Administer Naloxone 0.1mg/kg IV every 5 minutes to restore respiratory drive to Max total 2mg
protocols.content:
Paramedic:
Begin advanced airway management as appropriate
Initiate cardiac monitoring
If signs of shock refer to Shock protocols
Patient exhibits signs of organophosphate poisoning
○ Administer Atropine 0.02mg/kg  IV/IO
▪ Repeat at 0.02mg/kg every 3 minutes fully atropinized (secretions dried)
Suspected TCA overdose
○ Administer Sodium Bicarbonate 1mEq/kg  IV/IO
Suspected beta-blocker overdose
○ Administer Glucagon 0.7mg/kg  IV/IO
▪ May repeat x1 to max of 5mg
Suspected calcium channel-blocker overdose
○ Administer Calcium chloride 20mg/kg  IV/IO (Max 1g)
May repeat x 1 after 10 minutes
Suspected dystonic reaction
○ Administer Diphenhydramine 1mg/kg (Max 50mg) IV/IO/IM
Suspected adrenal crisis
AMS, hypoglycemia, hypotension, seizures, arrhythmias

protocols.title: Administer Solu-Medrol 2mg/kg IV/IO/IM
protocols.content:
Indications:
An apparent life-threatening event (ALTE) is defined as an episode that is frightening to the observer and is characterized by some combination of:
Apnea
Color change
Marked change in muscle tone
Unexplained choking or gagging

protocols.title: A brief resolved unexplained event (BRUE) is similar to ALTE but symptoms resolve without intervention
protocols.content:
Basic Care:
Consult age based guide, such as Handtevy app, for appropriate medication doses/interventions/equipment sizes and reference to normal vital sign ranges for pediatric patients
Provide emotional support to parents
Document all aspects of scene and environmental conditions
If Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS) is suspected, consult cardiac arrest protocols (See Page 79)
Monitor ABC’s and assessment using the Pediatric Assessment Triangle
Measure and record temperature
Blow-by oxygen as tolerated
Pulse oximetry for reported apneic events
Determine blood glucose concentration
ALL infants who have experienced an ALTE or BRUE must be transported to the appropriate children’s hospital

protocols.title: (Ped. Assessment Triangle)
protocols.content:
Indications:
Exacerbation of previously diagnosed asthma
Characterized by some combination of:
Wheezing
Tachypnea
Accessory muscle use / retraction
Inability to speak in full sentences

protocols.title: Wheezing due to suspected asthma (>1 year of age)
protocols.content:
Basic Care:
Consult age based guide, such as Handtevy app, for appropriate medication doses/interventions/equipment sizes and reference to normal vital sign ranges for pediatric patients
Administer oxygen
Titrate to >95% and improved work of breathing
Initiate continuous EtCO2 monitoring
Wheezing/ bronchospasm:
Administer 0.5% Albuterol 2.5mg
May repeat x 1
May co-administer with 0.02% Ipratropium Bromide 0.5mg
Moderate to severe respiratory distress

protocols.title: Assist ventilations as necessary
protocols.content:
Advanced Care:
Moderate to severe respiratory distress:
Initiate CPAP per CPAP procedure
If signs of impending respiratory failure prior to or following administration of CPAP, proceed to assisted ventilations with BVM
Discontinue CPAP if patient becomes hypotensive
Establish IV/IO access with isotonic crystalloid solution to keep vein open

protocols.title: Additional DuoNeb doses may be given by the A-EMT as long as wheezing is present every 5 minutes to max of 3 additional doses
protocols.content:
Paramedic:
Initiate cardiac monitoring
Subacute presentation
Administer methylprednisolone 2mg/kg  IV/IO  - Max 125mg
Administer magnesium sulfate 50mg/kg (max 2g) infused over 10 minutes
Unable to cooperate/ tolerate nebulizer therapy or impending respiratory failure:
Administer Epinephrine (1:1000) 0.15mg IM
May repeat x 1 after 5 minutes
Symptoms increase in severity and respiratory failure suspected:

protocols.title: Initiate Pediatric Respiratory Distress or Failure protocol (See p.83)
protocols.content:
Indications:
Heart rate is less than age-appropriate rate with a pulse and signs of hypoperfusion, including hypotension

protocols.title: Pediatric symptomatic bradycardia most commonly results from inadequate oxygenation/ ventilation
protocols.content:
Basic Care:
Manage airway, breathing, and oxygenation as indicated
Titrate oxygen to a SpO2 > 95%
Begin / continue CPR for pediatric patients with a heart rate < 60 bpm and signs of hypoperfusion despite adequate oxygenation / ventilation
Place patient in supine or recovery position as indicated and tolerated by patient

protocols.title: Obtain a complete set of vital signs, including: SpO2 and blood glucose concentration.
protocols.content:
Advanced Care:
Initiate cardiac monitoring and obtain a 12-lead ECG if possible

protocols.title: Establish IV / IO access with isotonic crystalloid solution to keep vein open
protocols.content:
Paramedic:
Initiate advanced airway management as indicated and be prepared for post-intubation hypotension and/or worsening bradycardia.
Transcutaneous pacing:
Contact medical control for pediatric transcutaneous pacing order.
TCP in pediatric patients should be considered if:
Reversible causes (e.g., hypoxia, hypoglycemia, opioid overdose) and medications (e.g., atropine, epinephrine) have been considered/delivered without desired effect.
Presence of 2nd degree Mobitz type II or 3rd degree heart block or patient has had a heart transplant.
Consider sedation prior to TCP, if the patient isn’t at risk of impending cardiovascular collapse, or if purposeful movement affects TCP
Recommended initial settings to request orders for:
Mode: syn/demand
Rate:
<1 yo: 120 bpm
1-10 yo: 100 bpm
≥11 yo: 80 bpm
Current: start low and increase by 5-10 mA until mechanical capture is achieved (usually 40-80 mA).
Generally, the above listed heart rates are enough to produce adequate perfusion.

protocols.title: If capture not achieved at current of 110 mA, consider repositioning pads and additional/alternative treatments.
protocols.content:
Special Considerations:
- Epinephrine:
First-line medication for pediatric symptomatic bradycardia.
0.01 mg/kg IV/IO slow IVP.  Repeat every 3-5 minutes as needed.
- Atropine:
Indicated for symptomatic bradycardia due to increased vagal tone +/- 1st degree heart block.
Ineffective for heart transplant patients, bradycardia due to hypoxia, 3rd degree heart block, and usually 2nd degree heart block.
0.02 mg/kg IV/IO (min single dose 0.1 mg, total max dose 1 mg).  Repeat every 3-5 minutes, as needed.
- Fluid Resuscitation:
IV fluids can be used to treat hypotension (see Hypoperfusion page 80), but should not delay or replace epinephrine or treatments that directly target suspected causes of bradycardia (e.g., atropine for increased vagal tone).
When indicated, administer 10-20 mL/kg Isotonic crystalloid IV/IO (repeat x1 as needed). Contact medical control for additional fluid bolus orders.
- Situations where additional/alternative treatments are often needed, include:
Beta blocker overdose:
Glucagon 0.05 mg/kg IV/IO (max single 5 mg) given over 1 minute.  Contact medical control for additional doses.
Calcium channel blocker overdose:
Calcium chloride 20 mg/kg IV/IO slow IVP.  Contact medical control for additional doses.
Hyperkalemia:
Calcium chloride 20 mg/kg IV/IO slow IVP.  Contact medical control for additional doses.
Sodium bicarbonate (8.4% solution) 1 mEq/kg IV/IO (4.2% solution recommended for <1 month old).  Repeat x1 in 5-10 minutes, as needed.
Severe / prolonged acidosis or sodium channel blocker overdose:
Sodium bicarbonate (8.4% solution) 1 mEq/kg IV/IO (4.2% solution recommended for <1 month old).  Repeat x1 in 5-10 minutes, as needed.
Symptomatic bradycardia refractory to TCP and/or other treatments:
Consider epinephrine infusion 0.1-1.0 mcg/min (see Epinephrine Infusion protocol page 132).
or

protocols.title: Consider push-dose Epinephrine 1 mcg/kg slow IVP over 2 minutes.  Repeat every 3-5 minutes, as needed
protocols.content:
Indications:
When the upper airway is infected with the virus that causes croup, tissues around the voice box (larynx) and the windpipe (trachea) will swell.
When a cough forces air through this narrowed passageway, it may sound like a seal barking.
Fever
Hoarse voice
Noisy or labored breathing

protocols.title: Often worse at night
protocols.content:
Basic Care:
Consult age-based guide, such as Handtevy app, for appropriate medication doses/interventions/equipment sizes and reference to normal vital sign ranges for pediatric patients
Administer oxygen
Titrate to >95% and improved work of breathing
Consider humidified oxygen for mild symptoms
Initiate EtCO2 monitoring
Remove any tight clothing
Allow patient to remain in a position of comfort with someone familiar
The condition of an upset patient can deteriorate quicker than that of a calm patient
Family should be used to soothe the patient and keep them calm if possible
Do not force the patient into a position, they will protect their airway by their positioning
Evaluation should include temperature

protocols.title: Passive cooling if patient found to be febrile
protocols.content:
Advanced Care:
Establish IV/IO access with isotonic crystalloid solution to keep vein open

protocols.title: Initiate cardiac monitoring if possible
protocols.content:
Paramedic:
For severe respiratory distress:

protocols.title: Administer nebulized epinephrine (1:1000) 3mg mixed with 3ml isotonic crystalloid solution
protocols.content:
Basic Care:
Consult age-based guide, such as Handtevy app, for appropriate medication doses/interventions/equipment sizes and reference to normal vital sign ranges for pediatric patients
Administer oxygen
Titrate to >95% and improved work of breathing
Initiate continuous EtCO2 monitoring
Determine blood glucose concentration
Relatively or clinically hypoglycemic without concern for aspiration
Administer oral glucose 15g buccal

protocols.title: May repeat every 5 minutes as needed
protocols.content:
Advanced Care & Paramedic:
Establish IV/IO access with isotonic crystalloid solution to keep vein open
Hyperglycemia:
Consider 250-500 ml fluid bolus as appropriate if no concern for respiratory status or pulmonary edema
Hypoglycemia:
Use D5W if available for IV/IO access
Administer Dextrose 10% 4ml/kg  IV/IO
OR if IV/IO access cannot be obtained, administer Glucagon

protocols.title: 0.1 mg/kg (max 1mg) IM
protocols.content:
Basic Care:
Consult age-based guide, such as Handtevy app, for appropriate medication doses/interventions/equipment sizes and reference to normal vital sign ranges for pediatric patients
Rectal temperature is the preferred method of obtaining core temperature in children
Begin passive cooling, remove excessive clothing/ blankets
Do not cool to induce shivering
Follow Pediatric Seizure protocol if febrile seizure is suspected
For temperatures > 100.5⁰ F
If a child has had Acetaminophen more than 4 hours prior
Administer Acetaminophen 15mg/kg PO (Max single dose 500mg)
If the last dose of Acetaminophen was less than 4 hours prior and the child has not had Ibuprofen in the previous 6 hours
Administer Ibuprofen 10mg/kg PO (Max single dose 300mg)

protocols.title: Contraindicated in children under 6 months of age
protocols.content:
Indications:
Elevated body temperature related to heat exposure

protocols.title: Altered mental status related to heat exposure
protocols.content:
Basic Care:
Consult age-based guide, such as Handtevy app, for appropriate medication doses/interventions/equipment sizes and reference to normal vital sign ranges for pediatric patients
Administer oxygen
Titrate to >95% and improved work of breathing
Initiate continuous EtCO2 monitoring
Move patient to a cool place away from any external heat sources if possible
Obtain patient temperature (rectal temperature is preferred in pediatrics if available)
Mild symptoms: (heat cramps, heat exhaustion, no signs of AMS, body temperature is <104 ⁰F
Help facilitate passive cooling
Loosen clothing, remove excessive clothing/ blankets
Administer PO fluids (if available and patient tolerates)
Discontinue if report of nausea/ vomiting
Determine blood glucose concentration
Severe symptoms: (signs of AMS, body temperature >104⁰ F, patient may or may not be sweating)
Begin active cooling
Transport may be delayed for on-scene cold water immersion if possible
Use sheets or towels dipped in ice water on exposed skin

protocols.title: Place ice packs behind neck, in axillae, and in groin areas
protocols.content:
Advanced Care:
Establish IV/IO access with isotonic crystalloid solution to keep vein open

protocols.title: Initiate IV/IO fluid bolus 20ml/kg for hypotension
protocols.content:
Paramedic:
Uncontrolled shivering during cooling

protocols.title: Administer Midazolam 0.1mg/kg (Max 1mg) IV/IO/IM/IN
protocols.content:
Indications:
Decreased body temperature related to cold exposure
Altered mental status related to cold exposure

protocols.title: Repeated ACLS medications and repeated defibrillations are ineffective below 86 degrees Fahrenheit (Core temperature)
protocols.content:
Basic Care:
Consult age-based guide, such as Handtevy app, for appropriate medication doses/interventions/equipment sizes and reference to normal vital sign ranges for pediatric patients
Administer oxygen
Titrate to >95% and improved work of breathing
Initiate continuous EtCO2 monitoring
Decrease on-going heat loss ASAP
Move the patient to a warm area
Dry and insulate the patient
Handle the patient gently, allowing the patient no exertion
Rough handling of a severely hypothermic patient may induce ventricular fibrillation
Remove all wet clothing (cut off to decrease patient movement)
Initiate passive external warming with blankets in a warm ambulance
Utilize heat blankets from blanket warmer device if available
Obtain patient temperature (core temperature preferred if obtainable)
Suspected hypothermia:
Assess respirations and pulse carefully as both may be very slow but still adequate for patient’s slowed metabolism
Provide expeditious, non-emergency transport
Call for ALS assistance, but DO NOT DELAY TRANSPORT
Begin airway management as appropriate
Follow other protocols as appropriate
Diabetic emergencies

protocols.title: Altered mental status/ overdose/ toxidrome
protocols.content:
Advanced Care & Paramedic:
Severe hypothermia:
If a shockable rhythm is present, administer only one defibrillatory shock
Establish IV/IO access with isotonic crystalloid solution to keep vein open
Cardiac arrest:

protocols.title: Administer Epinephrine (1:10000) 0.01 mg/kg (max one dose) IV/IO
protocols.content:
Basic Care:
Consult age-based guide, such as Handtevy app, for appropriate medication doses/interventions/equipment sizes and reference to normal vital sign ranges for pediatric patients
Gently position the patient to facilitate the airway

protocols.title: Suction as necessary
protocols.content:
Advanced Care:
Establish IV/IO access with isotonic crystalloid solution to keep vein open
Signs/ symptoms of volume depletion:
Consider administration of isotonic solution fluid bolus 20ml/kg IV/IO
Consider possible causes and follow other protocols as appropriate for:
Trauma
Abdominal pain
Altered mental status/ overdose/ toxidrome
Mild to moderate nausea /vomiting:
Administer Ondanestron 0.1 mg/kg IV/IO OR 4 mg SL (If > 4 years of age)

protocols.title: May repeat x 1 after 10 minutes
protocols.content:
Paramedic:
Severe nausea/ vomiting

protocols.title: Administer Droperidol 0.01 mg/kg (Max 1.25 mg) IV/IO/IM
protocols.content:
Basic Care:
Consult age-based guide, such as Handtevy app, for appropriate medication doses/interventions/equipment sizes and reference to normal vital sign ranges for pediatric patients. Remember to obtain a blood glucose assessment from heel stick during continued assessment.
Once the body is fully delivered, dry the infant and wrap in a thermal blanket or dry towel. Cover the infant’s scalp.
Assess breathing
If breathing is inadequate, stimulate the infant by gently rubbing the back and flicking the soles of the feet

Assist ventilations

protocols.title: Discontinue fluids if patient develops sign/symptoms of volume overload (e.g., new/worsening tachypnea, SOA, decreasing SpO2, new/worsening rales/crackles).

protocols.title: Instructions
protocols.content:
Expose the patient’s chest and prepare the area as necessary, being mindful of modesty and patient comfort.  Consider utilizing a hospital gown to protect privacy.  Shave the area if needed.
Apply the chest and extremity leads using the following landmarks:
RA – 	Right arm
LA – 	Left arm
RL – 	Right Leg
LL – 	Left Leg
V1 - 	4th intercostal space at the right sternal border
V2 - 	4th intercostal space at the left sternal border
V3 - 	Directly between V2 & V4
V4 - 	5th intercostal space at the midclavicular line

protocols.title: Transmit data ahead to PCI centers as appropriate to alert for potential activation of cath lab
protocols.content:
Instructions
Attach oxygen supply lines to driving gas input on rear of device and to oxygen tank or fixed regulator
Select vent settings
For Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP)
Start PEEP/CPAP dial at 5-10 cm H2O
Start Peak Pressure dial to 25 cm H2O
Set Mandatory Breath switch to off
Set %Oxygen switch to 100%
In CPAP mode – the tidal volume and respiratory rate dials do not affect the functionality of the unit.  They are overridden when the mandatory breath switch is in the off position
Titrate all settings as patient condition indicates
For post intubation ventilation
Start PEEP/ CPAP dial at 5-10 cm H2O
Start Peak Pressure dial to 25 cm H2O
Tidal volume dial - Calculate 6-8 mL/kg (ideal body weight) up to 700 mL for initial setting
Set respiratory rate dial to 10-12
Set %Oxygen switch to 100%
Set Mandatory breath switch to on
Titrate all settings as patient condition indicates
Attach patient circuit tubing to the expiratory valve and patient connection port
Attach in line nebulizer T-piece if needed
Attach EtCO2 to all connections
Attach the terminal end of the patient circuit to patient
For CPAP
Attach to CPAP mask and secure to patients face with adequate seal using adjustable face straps
Ensure comfort and compliance with the patient
For Intubated patients
Attach to Endotracheal tube, I-Gel, SGA
Ensure EtCO2 waveform is recorded
Monitor patient for improvement/ deterioration
Titrate vent settings as indicated by patient condition
WARNINGS & CONTRAINDICATIONS
The ventilator does not have an audible alarm to indicate it has been disconnected from the patient.  Monitor the patient closely.
Do not use in patients undergoing procedures with flammable anesthetic gases
Do not use in patients undergoing hyperbaric treatment
Tidal volume and peak pressure dials set greater than recommended settings may cause barotrauma
Do not use for any patient below 50 pounds (23kg)

protocols.title: Do not use in infants or neonatal patients or patients requiring volumes less than 360 mL
protocols.content:
Instructions
Hyperextend the head of the patient
Test the cuff by inserting 10 mL of air and withdrawing
Locate the cricothyroid membrane by palpation of the depressions between the thyroid and cricoid cartilage.  Stabilize this point with index finger and thumb for puncture
Puncture the cricothyroid membrane at a 90⁰ angle
Due to the sharp and conical needle tip, a prior incision is not necessary.  The opening of the trachea is obtained by dilation which reduces the risk of bleeding
Insert the Quicktrach II in a 45⁰ angle further towards the trachea up to the stopper
The stopper helps to prevent the needle from being inserted too deep, helping to avoid a possible perforation of the rear tracheal wall
Aspirate air with the syringe to determine the position of the cannula. If this is possible, the needle tip is correctly placed in the trachea
Remove the stopper from the cannula
Push the plastic cannula forward with the thumb until the safety clip audibly clicks into position
This indicates the tip of the metal needle is covered by the plastic cannula to prevent trauma
Further insert the Quicktrach II until the flange rests on the neck
Remove metal needle from the cannula and discard in sharps container
Inflate the cuff with the prepared syringe (10mL air). Check for proper inflation of the pilot balloon.
Secure the plastic cannula to the neck with the foam neck tape

protocols.title: Ventilate the patient directly via the 15 mm standard connector or via the included connecting tube.
protocols.content:
Instructions
Perform a physical assessment to determine the need for imminent delivery or need for immediate transport. Visualize the vaginal opening to observe for normal birth presentation or one of the below conditions.
Conditions that prompt need for immediate transport despite the threat of imminent delivery include: breech presentation, cord prolapse, extremity presentation, meconium staining, nuchal cord
See Obstetric emergencies protocol for any of the above (Page 36)
Try to obtain information such as:

Instructions
When necessary, EMS shall restrain combative or disoriented patients who present a physical danger to themselves or others
Mildly combative or disoriented patients may be restrained if there is reason for concern that a worsening of the patient’s condition may present a physical danger to themselves or others
Extremely violent patients may require the assistance of law enforcement to facilitate restraint
Consider that aggressive behavior may be a sign of a medical condition that requires medical intervention
If unable to verbally de-escalate the situation, and the scene is unsafe, or if the patient has any type of weapon, withdraw from the scene to a safe location and wait for law enforcement to secure the scene and request your return
The patient shall be restrained in a supine position ONLY.  Prone positioning is not acceptable under any circumstances.
Stretcher straps, spine board straps are appropriate means of securing a patient to the stretcher
Commercial soft restraints or cravats may be utilized to secure the patient’s arms and legs to the stretcher
Prior to and immediately following the application of physical restraints, the crew will complete an assessment of pulse, motor, and sensory of the limb distal to the restraints
The use of a spit hood is appropriate when needed to protect the crew from infectious diseases and possible blood-borne pathogens
Any use of any restraint not authorized in the policy is strictly prohibited.  Examples include but are not limited to:
Tape, Rope, Binding Materials, Choke holds
WARNING!
Overstepping the boundaries of legal restraint, may be perceived as battery, assault, a violation of civil rights, or false imprisonment
KRS 503.110 – Use of force by person with responsibility for care, discipline, or safety of others
The use of physical force by a defendant upon another person is justifiable when the defendant is a person responsible for the operation or the maintenance of order in a vehicle or other carrier of passengers and the defendant believes that such force is necessary to prevent interference with its operation or to maintain order in the vehicle or other carrier, except that deadly physical force may be used only when the defendant believes it necessary to prevent death or serious physical injury
The use of physical force by a defendant upon another person is justifiable when the defendant is a doctor or other therapist or a person assisting him at his direction, and:
The force is used for the purpose of administering a recognized form of treatment which the defendant believes to be adapted to promoting the physical or mental health of the patient, AND
The treatment is administered with the consent of the patient or, if the patient is a minor or a mentally disabled person, with the consent of the parent, guardian, or other person legally competent to consent in his behalf, or the treatment is administered in an emergency when the defendant believes that no one competent to consent can be consulted and that a reasonable person, wishing to safeguard the welfare of the patient, would consent.
The goal is to prevent unnecessary immobilization while still protecting patients at risk for spinal injury.
The need for full spinal immobilization is diminishing and is a tool that is only indicated in certain clinical situations and requires provider judgement. Risks of full immobilization include increased pain, pressure ulcers, respiratory complications and should be utilized for extrication, or if rapid transport or patient condition is requires. Examples would include emergent transports to the Level 1 trauma center, or distracting injuries [e.g., large surface burns, long bone fractures, spinal deformity crush injuries.]
Consider selective spinal immobilization when you have high energy mechanism injuries, patient presentation indicates spinal precautions are needed, or you have any of the following:
Altered Mental Status or Evidence of Intoxication
Midline back pain or tenderness
Neuroligical complaints of acute numbness or weakness
An age over 8 and under 65, as the other age groups fall into special populations.
OR
Axial Load Injuries
Blunt trauma to head from fall/ MVA
Impact from sport injuries
Any other traumatic head/neck complaints
**If a scoop stretcher or backboard was used for extrication and is appropriate, remove the device for positioning and comfort on the stretcher.
Steps for Selective Immobilization
Start by maintaining manual inline stabilization and then apply a rigid cervical collar that fits your patient.
Minimize movements and transfers of the patient while adequately securing the patient to the stretcher.
These patients are not to be upright walking or sitting in Fowler's position.
Maintain inline stabilization during any patient movement or transfer.
Penetrating Trauma to the neck does not require spinal immobilization unless there are new neurological deficits noted or spinal deformity.
C-Spine Clearance
Immobilization is not required in all traumatic events.
Is the patient alert, oriented, at their baseline without signs of intoxication?
Are there any distracting injuries?
Are there any abnormal findings during neurological assessments such as numbness, change in sensation, or paralysis?
Is there any reports of midline tenderness of the neck or back?
Is there any pain with flexion/extension of the neck or rotation in any direction?
**If the answer to the following questions is no, following Nexus criteria immobilization is not required however use provident judgement.

protocols.title: Law enforcement agencies may use a conductive energy device called a taser.  This device is a less-lethal tool.  When used, the device discharges a wire that contains, at the distal end, an arrow-like barbed projectile that penetrates the suspect’s skin and embeds itself.  This allows the officer to administer an incapacitating electrical shock.  Officers may initiate an EMS response when the device is discharged.  The most common injuries from taser use are trauma from a fall due the person’s sudden incapacitation.
protocols.content:
Instructions
Before touching any patient who has been subdued using a taser, EMS personnel shall ensure the officer has disconnected the wires from the handheld unit
In most cases, the wires will have been cut prior to EMS arrival
Provide routine assessment of injuries, vitals, patient specific complaints
Identify the location of the probes in the patient’s body
If a probe is embedded in the patient’s head, face, neck, groin, or spine, EMS MUST TRANSPORT to an emergency department
Confer with the officer and determine the patient’s condition from the time of the taser discharge to the arrival of EMS
Consider medical conditions which may be the underlying cause of the situation
Obtain a history of the last tetanus shot
Remove barbs by applying firm tension to the skin, pulling it taught, while simultaneously pulling the barbs perpendicular to the body/ skin
Dispose of barbs in a sharps container or provide to law enforcement if they are requested
Clean the puncture site and bandage
Unless the patient has a cardiac complaint or underlying medical condition related to suspected dysrhythmia, a 12 lead ECG is not required
